significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish a form-(iii) relation—“binding-error rate ... grows with item similarity and context length”—together with a causal decomposition in which rerouting an item-binding representation repairs belief errors without changing the truth-value representation. Feng and Steinhardt’s How Do Language Models Bind Entities in Context? (ICLR 2024) makes entity–attribute binding a consequential internal computation; the proposed conclusion would specifically predict which ambiguous belief queries fail and whether rebinding rather than truth steering should repair them. The phenomenon is the similarity- and context-dependent misattribution of beliefs, while the mechanism is the separable item–truth binding whose intervention yields a double dissociation; a negative result on that decomposition would rule out binding as a common explanation, although the claim’s multiple subclaims permit mixed outcomes. Verified-true and verified-false states are distinguishable, and the topic-substitution check fails: generic research on LLM beliefs would not itself imply binding errors, their scaling relation, or the binding-versus-truth intervention distinction.

reach.justification: The named handles are the “binding-error rate,” an “item-conditioned belief probe,” and an “attention-based re-binding intervention.” Because probe-detected misbinding is claimed to be “predictive of behavioral belief errors” from query-position activations, it can operate ex ante—before the answer is produced—and the rerouting intervention gives auditors or deployment systems an action to take rather than merely a post-hoc explanation. Exact probes and subspaces would require re-extraction per model, but the asserted relation that errors grow with item similarity and context length predicts a transferable trend; the intervention itself is less portable and likely needs model-specific calibration. The asserted scope is multi-item referentially ambiguous LLM contexts rather than all belief failures, but it can still inform researchers and practitioners who screen or gate such prompts; the topic-substitution check fails because the belief topic alone supplies none of these diagnostics, forecasts, or interventions.
